theme: God calls Samuel; the ark captured; Ichabod
readingInstruction: Read 1 Samuel 3:1-4:22. These chapters tell how God called Samuel and how the ark was lost in battle. Notice how the word of the LORD comes to a child and how Israel treats the ark as a charm.
settingTheScene: The word of the LORD was rare in those days, and visions were not widespread (3:1). Samuel, still a boy, serves in the sanctuary under Eli. The scenes that follow show God breaking the silence, and then a terrible defeat when Israel goes to war against the Philistines. The chapters belong together: in the first, the word of God is heard, and in the second, it is ignored, with disastrous results.
observation: The lamp of God had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying down in the temple of the LORD where the ark was (3:3).
The LORD calls “Samuel!” three times, and Samuel thinks it is Eli (3:4-8).
Eli tells him to answer, “Speak, LORD, for your servant hears” (3:9).
God tells Samuel that he will judge Eli’s house forever, “because his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them” (3:13).
Eli says, “It is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him” (3:18).
“And all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established as a prophet of the LORD” (3:20).
Israel is defeated by the Philistines and brings the ark of the covenant from Shiloh, and the Philistines hear the shout and are afraid (4:1-7).
The ark is captured, Hophni and Phinehas are killed, Eli falls and dies, and Phinehas’ wife names her son Ichabod, “The glory has departed from Israel” (4:10-22).
interpretation:
The call of Samuel is among the most loved stories in Scripture, and it carries a sharp lesson. “Samuel did not yet know the LORD, and the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him.” He served in the sanctuary, but he had not yet been addressed by God. Religious activity is not the same as hearing God. The LORD takes the initiative, and he calls a child.

Eli’s response is a mixture of failure and faithfulness. He was a poor father who let his sons go unchecked. Yet when Samuel is called, Eli tells him the right words, “Speak, LORD, for your servant hears.” Even a flawed leader can point someone toward God. And when he hears the word of judgment, he accepts it humbly. There is something moving in his submission, though it does not erase his guilt.

Samuel’s first prophetic task is heavy: to tell his master that judgment is coming. He is afraid. But Eli asks him to speak plainly, and he does. This is the first test of a prophet: to say what God says, even when it is hard.

Chapter 4 shows the cost of ignoring the word. Israel loses a battle, and instead of repenting, the elders decide to bring the ark, as though it were a lucky charm. “Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD here from Shiloh, that it may come among us and save us from the power of our enemies.” They treat God’s presence as a tool. The Philistines are afraid, but God does not fight for people who use him. Israel is crushed, the ark is taken, and the corrupt priests die.

The name Ichabod captures the meaning: “The glory has departed.” It is the lowest point in the story so far. But the God who is not bound to an object will soon show his power in Philistia.
connection: Jesus said, “Whoever is of God hears the words of God” (John 8:47), and “My sheep hear my voice” (John 10:27). James 1:22 calls us to be doers of the word. Jeremiah 7:12-14 points back to Shiloh as a warning not to trust in the temple. Hebrews 1:1-2 says that God, who spoke in many ways, has now spoken by his Son.
application:
Pray Samuel’s prayer, “Speak, LORD, for your servant hears,” before your next time in Scripture.

Ask whether you treat any religious object, place, or habit as a charm.

If someone has said a hard word to you from God’s Word, consider listening with Eli’s humility.
prayerPrompts: Pray, “Speak, LORD, your servant hears,” and then listen for a moment.
Ask him to keep you from treating his presence as a tool.
Thank him for the Word made flesh.
